intro: Buddhists do not only read their scriptures. They live them. They keep festivals through the year. They meet in temples to chant, listen and share food. In this unit, you will visit Buddhist festivals and communities, from Asia to Chicago.
First you will learn about Vesak, Hanamatsuri, Uposatha, Kathina, Obon and Losar. Then you will learn how Buddhist temples began in Chicago and what you might see if you visit one.
By the end, you will be able to name the main Buddhist festivals and tell what each remembers. You will be able to describe a temple visit and explain how to be a respectful guest.
bigQuestion: How do Buddhist festivals and temples help people remember the Buddha and care for each other?

write.prompt: Pick two Buddhist festivals from this unit. What does each one help Buddhists remember? Use one story or text from the unit, like the Vinaya's rains rule or the Ullambana Sutra, and tell how Buddhists keep the day.
tips: Name the festival and the country or tradition that keeps it.
Say 'Buddhists believe' or 'the story tells' when you tell a belief.
Name the text you use, like the Vinaya or the Ullambana Sutra.
Use unit words like sangha, merit and offerings.

title: Festivals and Communities

chapters.title: Vesak, Obon and the Buddhist Year
chapters.bigQuestion: How do Buddhist festivals help families remember the Buddha and each other?

story.title: Sweet Tea for a Tiny Statue
story.kicker: Children line up in a temple full of flowers to pour tea over a very small statue.
paragraphs: It is a spring morning in a Japanese American temple. The room smells of flowers. Near the front is a tiny roof made of blossoms. Under the roof stands a small statue of a baby. The baby points one hand up and one hand down.
A girl named Emi waits in line with her little brother. Her grandmother holds their coats. When Emi reaches the front, she picks up a small wooden ladle. She dips it into a bowl of sweet tea.
Emi pours the tea gently over the statue. Her brother does the same. Their grandmother bows her head. She tells them this day is called Hanamatsuri, the Flower Festival.

Buddhists in Japan keep this day to remember the birth of the Buddha. Their stories say he was born in a garden full of flowers. After the pouring, the children drink a cup of the sweet tea. Then everyone shares lunch.
story.think: Why do you think families pour tea over the statue instead of just looking at it?

lessons.title: Vesak: Three Events, One Day
lessons.mainIdea: Many Buddhists keep Vesak to remember the Buddha's birth, awakening and death all on one day.
reading: In Sri Lanka, Thailand and many other places, a big holiday comes in spring. It is called *Vesak*. Some people spell it Wesak. It falls on the full moon of a month in April or May.
Many Theravada Buddhists teach that three things happened on this same full moon. The Buddha was born. He reached awakening under a tree. Many years later, he died. So Vesak remembers all three.

On Vesak, families visit the temple. They bring flowers and light lamps. Many take the five promises called *precepts* for the day. Streets fill with lanterns. Some people give free food to anyone who walks by.

words.d: a Buddhist holiday in spring that remembers the Buddha's birth, awakening and death
promises Buddhists make about how to act, such as not harming and not lying

look.title: A Street on Vesak Night
look.text: Picture a street in Colombo, Sri Lanka, on Vesak night. Paper lanterns shaped like stars hang from every house. A big painted board shows a story of the Buddha's past life. A family hands out cups of tea and rice to people walking by.
look.prompt: Name two things in this picture that show giving. Why might giving fit a holiday about the Buddha?

check.q: What three events do many Buddhists remember on Vesak?
choices: The Buddha's birth, awakening and death
The first rice harvest, the rains and the new year
The building of three famous temples
check.why: Many Theravada Buddhists teach that the Buddha's birth, awakening and death all fell on the Vesak full moon.

check.q: When does Vesak usually come?
choices: On the first snow of winter
On a full moon in April or May
On the shortest day of the year
check.why: Vesak follows the moon, so it lands on a full moon in April or May.

check.q: Which is something families often do on Vesak?
choices: Stay home and keep the lights off
Take part in a race around the city
Light lamps and bring flowers to the temple
Cut down a tree for the house
check.why: Lamps, flowers and temple visits are common Vesak customs.

lessons.title: Bathing the Baby Buddha
lessons.mainIdea: In Japan and other places, Buddhists remember the Buddha's birth by pouring sweet tea over a small statue.
reading: In Japan, the Buddha's birthday is often kept on April 8. The day is called *Hanamatsuri*, which means Flower Festival. Temples build a small shrine covered in flowers.
Inside stands a statue of the baby Buddha. Buddhist stories say that right after he was born, he took seven steps. He pointed up to the sky and down to the earth. The statue shows him that way.

People pour sweet tea over the statue with a ladle. Many say this remembers a story that the heavens sent gentle rain to wash the new baby. Korean, Chinese and Taiwanese Buddhists also bathe the baby Buddha on his birthday.

words.d: the Flower Festival in Japan, when Buddhists remember the Buddha's birth
a special place set up to honor a holy person or thing

look.title: The Birth in a Garden
look.text: The old story tells that Queen Maya stopped to rest in the Lumbini garden. There, under a flowering tree, she gave birth to her son. Later tellings add that the baby stepped forward and spoke.
look.cite: Retold from the Nidanakatha, the opening of the Jataka commentary; tr. T.W. Rhys Davids, Buddhist Birth Stories (1880)
look.prompt: Why do you think the Japanese festival uses so many flowers?

check.q: What does Hanamatsuri mean?
check.why: Hana means flower, and the festival fills a small shrine with blossoms.

check.q: What do people pour over the baby Buddha statue?
check.why: At Hanamatsuri, people ladle sweet tea over the small statue.

check.q: How does the statue of the baby Buddha often stand?
choices: One hand points up and one points down
He is lying asleep in a bed
check.why: Buddhist stories say the newborn pointed up to the sky and down to the earth.

lessons.title: Different Lands, Different Calendars
lessons.mainIdea: Buddhists in different countries keep the Buddha's birthday on different dates.
reading: Not every Buddhist keeps the Buddha's birthday on the same day. Many Theravada countries use a moon calendar. So Vesak moves a little each year. Some use the sun instead.
In Japan, most temples use April 8 on the modern calendar. In Korea, China and Taiwan, many keep the eighth day of the fourth moon month. That day falls in April or May.

This does not mean one group is right. Each community follows its own *calendar*. A *lunar* calendar counts months by the moon. Families in Illinois may keep the day of the country their family came from.

words.d: a way of counting days, months and years
about the moon; a lunar calendar counts months by the moon

look.title: When the Birthday Is Kept
look.cite: Common festival calendars; moon dates move each year
look.prompt: Which country uses a fixed date? Why do the others move?

check.q: Why does Vesak move a little each year?
choices: The king picks a new day each year
It is always on a Monday
check.why: Vesak is set by the full moon, so its date changes on the regular calendar.

check.q: What does lunar mean?
check.why: A lunar calendar counts months by the moon.

check.q: Which is the best way to describe different birthday dates?
choices: Each community follows its own calendar
One country has the only right date
Nobody knows what a calendar is
check.why: Different Buddhist communities use different calendars, and none is ranked above the others.

lessons.title: Uposatha: Moon Days
lessons.mainIdea: Uposatha days are moon days when many Buddhists visit the temple and keep extra promises.
reading: Some Buddhist holy days come every week or two. They are called *Uposatha* days. They follow the phases of the moon, like the full moon and the new moon.

On these days, many Theravada laypeople go to the temple. A *layperson* is a Buddhist who is not a monk or nun. They listen to a talk and give food. Some keep eight promises instead of five for that day.
Monks meet on the full moon and new moon days too. The Vinaya, the book of rules for monks and nuns, says they gather to recite their rules together. It is a way to keep the community honest.

words.d: a Buddhist moon day for temple visits, teaching and keeping extra promises
a Buddhist who is not a monk or nun

look.title: A Moon Day at the Temple
look.text: It is a full moon Sunday at a Thai temple. An older woman wears white clothes. She brings a bowl of rice and fruit. She sits with others to hear a monk give a short talk. She will not eat again until the next morning.
look.prompt: What clues tell you this is a special day for her?

check.q: What are Uposatha days tied to?
check.why: Uposatha days follow the full moon, new moon and other moon phases.

check.q: What is a layperson?
choices: A monk who leads the temple
A Buddhist who is not a monk or nun
check.why: Laypeople are Buddhists who live ordinary home lives, not as monks or nuns.

check.q: What do monks do together on full and new moon days, as the Vinaya says?
check.why: The Vinaya describes monks meeting on these days to recite their rules.

lessons.title: Kathina: Robes for Monks
lessons.mainIdea: At Kathina, laypeople give cloth for robes to monks after the rainy season retreat.
reading: In the rainy season, many Theravada monks stay in one temple for about three months. This is the rains *retreat*. The Vinaya tells the story of why: walking in the rain could crush young plants and small creatures.
When the retreat ends, families hold a festival called *Kathina*. They bring cloth for new robes. They also bring food, soap and other things monks need.
People often walk in a happy line, carrying the gifts. For many Buddhists, giving is a way to make merit. Merit is the good that Buddhists believe comes from good actions.

words.d: a time when monks stay in one place to study and meditate
a festival after the rains retreat when laypeople give robe cloth to monks
the good that Buddhists believe comes from good actions like giving

look.title: Why Monks Stay Put
look.text: The Vinaya tells that people complained when monks walked about in the rains, treading on green plants and small living things. So the Buddha set a rule that monks should stay in one place for the rainy season.
look.cite: Vinaya Pitaka, Mahavagga III.1; see Rhys Davids and Oldenberg, Vinaya Texts, Sacred Books of the East 13 (1882)
look.prompt: What does this story show about the reason for the rule?

check.q: What do laypeople mostly give at Kathina?
check.why: Kathina is the time laypeople give robe cloth to monks.

check.q: When does Kathina happen?
choices: At the start of winter snow
check.why: Kathina comes after the roughly three-month rains retreat.

check.q: According to the Vinaya story, why do monks stay in one place in the rains?
choices: Because they are not allowed outside at all
So they do not tread on young plants and small creatures
Because the roads close for festivals
check.why: The Vinaya says the rule came from worry about crushing plants and small living things.

lessons.title: Lanterns, Flowers and Gifts
lessons.mainIdea: Lamps, flowers and incense are common offerings, and Buddhists give them meaning.
reading: At many festivals, people bring *offerings* to the shrine. Common ones are flowers, candles or lamps, incense and food. These gifts show respect for the Buddha. Each one is placed with care on the shrine table.
Buddhists often explain what each gift means. A lamp can stand for wisdom that lights the way. Fresh flowers wilt in a few days, so many teachers say they remind people that all things change.
Some offerings are also shared. Food given to the temple often feeds monks and guests. In this way, a festival is also a time for a whole *community* to eat together.

words.d: gifts people place at a shrine to show respect
a group of people who share a place, a practice or a life together

look.title: A Shrine Table
look.text: Look at a shrine table in a temple. In the middle is a statue of the Buddha. In front are a vase of yellow flowers, two candles, a small bowl of rice and a stick of incense. A thin line of smoke rises slowly.
look.prompt: Pick one offering. What might a Buddhist say it means?

check.q: Which is a common offering at a Buddhist shrine?
check.why: Flowers, candles, incense and food are common offerings.

check.q: What do many Buddhist teachers say fresh flowers remind people of?
check.why: Flowers wilt, so teachers often use them to point to change.

check.q: What often happens to food given at a festival?
choices: It is sold at a store
It is buried in the garden
check.why: Festival food is often shared by the temple community.

lessons.title: Obon: Welcoming Ancestors
lessons.mainIdea: At Obon, Japanese Buddhists honor family members who have died, with lanterns and dancing.
reading: In summer, many Japanese and Japanese American Buddhists keep *Obon*. It is a time to remember *ancestors*, the family members who lived before us. Many families keep it in July or August.

Families clean graves and set out food. Many light lanterns. At temples, people join in circle dances called Bon Odori. Buddhist temples in Chicago and across America hold Obon festivals, and neighbors are welcome.

Obon connects to a story. A student of the Buddha named Moggallana, called Mokuren in Japan, saw that his mother was suffering after death. The Buddha taught him to make offerings to monks to help her. The story says she was freed, and he danced for joy.

words.d: a summer Buddhist festival in Japan and Japanese America that honors ancestors
family members who lived long ago, like great-grandparents

look.title: The Story Behind Obon
look.text: A disciple sees his dead mother hungry and suffering. He asks the Buddha for help. The Buddha tells him to give food and gifts to the monks at the end of the rains retreat. By this merit, the sutra says, his mother is set free.
look.cite: Retold from the Ullambana Sutra (Chinese, c. 5th–6th century CE)
look.prompt: How does this story explain why people give and dance at Obon?

check.q: Who does Obon honor?
check.why: Obon is a time to remember family members who have died.

check.q: What is Bon Odori?
check.why: Bon Odori is the dance held at Obon festivals.

check.q: In the Obon story, who is Mokuren trying to help?
check.why: The story tells that Mokuren helped free his suffering mother.

lessons.title: Losar: Tibetan New Year
lessons.mainIdea: Losar is the Tibetan New Year, a time for cleaning, prayer flags, family and fresh starts.
reading: Tibetan Buddhists keep a new year festival called *Losar*. It follows a Tibetan moon calendar. It usually comes in February or March. Families look forward to it all winter.

Before Losar, families clean the house to sweep out the old year. They make special foods and fried pastries. Many hang new *prayer flags*. These are colored cloth flags printed with prayers and blessings.
On Losar, people visit monasteries and make offerings. They greet family and friends and wish them a good year. Tibetan families in America keep Losar too, often at a community center or temple.

words.d: the Tibetan New Year festival
colored cloth flags printed with prayers, hung by Tibetan Buddhists

look.title: Flags in the Wind
look.text: Five colors of flags hang on a string between two poles: blue, white, red, green and yellow. Each flag has words printed on it. When the wind blows, the flags flap. Tibetan Buddhists say the wind carries the blessings out to all beings.
look.prompt: Why might people hang new flags at the start of a new year?

check.q: What is Losar?
check.why: Losar is Tibetan New Year.

check.q: What do families do before Losar to get ready?
check.why: Cleaning sweeps out the old year before Losar.

check.q: What do Tibetan Buddhists say the wind does with prayer flags?
choices: Carries the blessings out to all beings
check.why: Tibetan Buddhists describe the wind spreading the printed blessings.

lessons.title: A Year of Festivals
lessons.mainIdea: Buddhist festivals follow the seasons and help communities share memory, giving and joy.
reading: Put the festivals together, and you see a whole *year*. Losar begins the year for Tibetans. The Buddha's birthday comes in spring. The rains retreat and Kathina follow the wet season.

Obon comes in summer. Uposatha moon days come all year round. Each festival fits a place and its weather. Some festivals are big and noisy. Others are quiet and simple. All of them help people remember.

Many Buddhists say festivals help them remember the Buddha's teachings. They also bring families together. A child may learn the stories best by joining the festival year after year, a tradition passed down.

words.d: the full circle of seasons, about 365 days
a way of doing things that is passed down from older people to younger people

look.title: A Festival Year
look.cite: Common festival calendars; many dates move with the moon
look.prompt: Which festival comes first in the calendar year? Which comes last?

check.q: Which festival usually comes in late fall, after the rains?
check.why: Kathina follows the end of the rains retreat, around October or November.

check.q: What is a tradition?
choices: A brand new rule made today
A way of doing things passed down over time
check.why: A tradition is handed from older people to younger people.

check.q: Which festival comes all year round?
check.why: Uposatha days follow the moon every month.

review.q: What does Vesak remember for many Theravada Buddhists?
choices: The end of the rains retreat
The Buddha's birth, awakening and death
review.why: Many Theravada Buddhists teach all three happened on the Vesak full moon.

review.q: At which festival do people pour sweet tea over a baby Buddha statue?
review.why: Hanamatsuri, the Flower Festival, includes bathing the baby Buddha.

choices: Laypeople give robe cloth to monks
review.why: Kathina is the robe-giving festival after the rains.
Obon remembers family members who have died.
Losar is the Tibetan New Year.

review.q: Why do Buddhist festival dates differ between countries?
choices: The festivals are chosen by a vote each year
review.why: Moon calendars and local customs set different dates.

review.q: What does merit mean to Buddhists?
choices: A prize for winning a race
The good that comes from good actions
The name of a monk's robe
review.why: Buddhists believe good actions like giving make merit.

review.q: Which book tells the rules for monks, including the rains retreat?
review.why: The Vinaya holds the rules for monks and nuns and the stories behind them.

chapters.title: Temples and Sanghas in Chicago
chapters.bigQuestion: What do Buddhist temples in Illinois show about how Buddhists live and practice together?

story.title: A New Temple in a New City
story.kicker: A family leaves a camp in 1944 and helps build a temple in Chicago.
paragraphs: During World War II, the U.S. government forced Japanese Americans on the West Coast to leave their homes. Families were sent to camps behind barbed wire. Many of these families were Buddhist.
In the camps, people still met for Buddhist services. They sat in plain wooden barracks. They chanted and listened to talks. A priest helped them keep their faith and their hope.
Some families were allowed to leave the camps if they moved away from the West Coast. Many came to Chicago. They found jobs and small apartments. But they missed their temple.
In 1944, a Buddhist priest named Gyomay Kubose and a group of Japanese Americans started a temple in Chicago. Today it is called the Buddhist Temple of Chicago. It still welcomes people every week.
story.think: Why might a temple matter so much to families who had lost their homes?

lessons.title: The Buddhist Temple of Chicago
lessons.mainIdea: Japanese Americans founded the Buddhist Temple of Chicago in 1944, after the wartime camps.
reading: The Buddhist Temple of Chicago began in 1944. Japanese Americans leaving the wartime *incarceration* camps started it. Incarceration means being locked up. These families had done nothing wrong.
The temple's first leader was Reverend Gyomay Kubose. He taught in plain English so everyone could understand. He wanted young Japanese Americans and new friends to feel welcome.
Today the temple stands in the Uptown neighborhood of Chicago. It holds Sunday services, classes and festivals. It is part of the long story of Buddhists in *Illinois*.

words.d: being locked up; in World War II, Japanese Americans were forced into camps
our state, home to many Buddhist temples and communities

look.title: Dates to Remember
look.cite: U.S. National Archives; Buddhist Temple of Chicago history
look.prompt: Was the temple started before or after the camps closed?

check.q: When did the Buddhist Temple of Chicago begin?
check.why: The temple was founded in 1944.

check.q: Who started the temple?
choices: Japanese Americans leaving the wartime camps
check.why: Japanese American families from the camps founded it with Rev. Gyomay Kubose.

check.q: What does incarceration mean?
check.why: Japanese Americans were forced into camps, which is incarceration.

lessons.title: Services in English
lessons.mainIdea: Many Japanese American temples hold Sunday services with chanting, a talk and music.
reading: Japanese American temples often hold services on Sunday. Many belong to a tradition called Jodo Shinshu, or *Shin Buddhism*. It centers on Amida Buddha.
At a service, people chant together. A minister gives a short talk, called a Dharma talk. Some temples have a Sunday school for children, too. Then people share tea and snacks.
Leaders like Rev. Kubose wanted the teaching in plain words. So many talks are in English. This helps children and new visitors understand the *Dharma*, the Buddha's teaching.

words.d: Jodo Shinshu, a Japanese Buddhist tradition centered on Amida Buddha
the Buddha's teaching (in Pali, dhamma)

look.title: A Sunday Morning
look.text: It is Sunday in a Chicago temple. Rows of chairs face a golden shrine. A minister rings a bell. People open small books and chant together. Then children go downstairs for Dharma school.
look.prompt: How is this like a gathering you know? How is it different?

check.q: What is a Dharma talk?
choices: A short talk about Buddhist teaching
check.why: A minister or teacher gives a Dharma talk about the Buddha's teaching.

check.q: Which Buddha is at the center of Shin Buddhism?
check.why: Jodo Shinshu centers on Amida Buddha.

check.q: Why did leaders like Rev. Kubose teach in English?
choices: So children and visitors could understand
check.why: He wanted the Dharma in plain words everyone could follow.

lessons.title: Chicago and 1893
lessons.mainIdea: In 1893, Buddhist teachers spoke in Chicago at the World's Parliament of Religions.
reading: Buddhism came to Chicago's attention long before 1944. In 1893, the city held a great world's fair. Beside it met the *World's Parliament of Religions*.
Leaders of many faiths spoke there. Anagarika Dharmapala came from Sri Lanka. Soyen Shaku, a Zen teacher, came from Japan. They explained Buddhism to large crowds.
Many Americans heard about Buddhist teaching for the first time. Some began to read Buddhist books. Chicago became an early *meeting place* of Buddhists and other Americans.

words.d: a big meeting of faith leaders held in Chicago in 1893
a place where different people come together

look.title: A Speaker in White
look.text: Picture a large hall in 1893. A young man from Sri Lanka stands up. He wears white robes. Thousands of people listen as he speaks about the Buddha. Many have never heard these ideas before.
look.prompt: What questions might the crowd have wanted to ask him?

check.q: Where was the World's Parliament of Religions held?
check.why: It met in Chicago in 1893.

check.q: Which Buddhist speaker came from Sri Lanka?
check.why: Dharmapala came from Sri Lanka; Soyen Shaku came from Japan.

check.q: In what year did the Parliament meet?
check.why: The World's Parliament of Religions met in 1893.

lessons.title: Temples from Many Lands
lessons.mainIdea: Illinois has Buddhist temples started by families from many Asian countries and by converts.
reading: Walk around Chicago and its suburbs, and you can find many kinds of Buddhist temples. Some were started by Thai families. Others by Vietnamese, Cambodian, Laotian, Sri Lankan, Korean, Chinese or Tibetan families.

Many of these families came to America after 1965, when the law made it easier to *immigrate*. Refugees from Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos came after wars in the 1970s. They built temples to keep their faith and language.
There are also *converts*. A convert is someone who chose a new religion. Some Americans who grew up in other faiths now meet in Zen or Tibetan Buddhist centers in Illinois.

words.d: to move to a new country to live
people who must leave their country to be safe
people who choose to join a new religion

look.title: Two Temples on One Street
look.text: On one street stands a Thai temple with a golden roof. Monks in orange robes walk in the yard. A few blocks away is a Vietnamese temple. A statue of the bodhisattva Quan Am, in white, stands in its garden.
look.prompt: What do these two temples show about Buddhism in Illinois?

check.q: What is a convert?
choices: Someone who chooses to join a new religion
check.why: A convert chooses a new religion, like some Americans who join Zen centers.

check.q: What happened in 1965 that helped many Asian families come to America?
choices: The first temple in Asia was built
A law made it easier to immigrate
check.why: The 1965 immigration law opened the way for many more Asian immigrants.

check.q: Who are refugees?
choices: People who must leave their country to be safe
check.why: Refugees, such as many from Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos, left to be safe.

lessons.title: Monks and Nuns
lessons.mainIdea: Monks and nuns give their lives to Buddhist practice, and laypeople support them.
reading: In many temples, you meet monks or nuns. They shave their heads and wear robes. The color can be orange, maroon, gray, brown or black, depending on the tradition.

Monks and nuns study, teach and meditate. In the Theravada tradition, they follow the many rules of the *Vinaya*. The community of monks and nuns is called the *sangha*. Some people use sangha for all Buddhists together.
Laypeople and the sangha help each other. Laypeople give food and needed things. Monks and nuns give teaching and lead ceremonies. Buddhists call this a circle of giving.

words.d: the community of monks and nuns; sometimes all Buddhists together
the part of the Buddhist scriptures with rules for monks and nuns

look.title: Robes of Many Colors
look.text: At an event in Chicago, monks and nuns from many temples stand together. Thai and Sri Lankan monks wear orange. Tibetan monks wear maroon and yellow. Korean nuns wear gray. Japanese Zen priests wear black.
look.prompt: Why might robe colors differ from country to country?

check.q: What is the sangha?
choices: The community of monks and nuns
check.why: Sangha names the Buddhist community, especially monks and nuns.

check.q: What do laypeople often give to monks and nuns?
check.why: Laypeople support the sangha with food and daily needs.

check.q: What do monks and nuns give in return?
check.why: The sangha offers teaching and leads ceremonies.

lessons.title: The Alms Round
lessons.mainIdea: In parts of Asia, monks walk each morning to receive food, and families feel glad to give.
reading: In Thailand, Laos, Cambodia and Myanmar, many monks walk out early each morning. They walk quietly in a line, carrying *alms bowls*. This is the alms round.
Families wait by the road. They place rice and other food in the bowls. Often they kneel or bow. The monks may chant a short blessing in return. No one hurries.
Monks do not ask for food. They simply walk. Buddhists say the round gives laypeople a chance to practice *generosity* every day. Some temples in America hold a version of this on special days.

words.d: bowls monks carry to receive food as a gift
being glad to give and share

look.title: Sunrise in Laos
look.text: The sky is pink. A line of monks in orange robes walks barefoot down a street. A grandmother kneels on a mat with a basket of sticky rice. She places a small ball of rice in each bowl as the monks pass.
look.prompt: What does the grandmother's kneeling show?

check.q: What do monks carry on the alms round?
check.why: Monks carry alms bowls to receive food.

check.q: How do monks get food on the alms round?
choices: They walk quietly and people give
They buy it at a store
They ask loudly at each door
check.why: Monks walk silently, and laypeople offer food.

check.q: What do Buddhists say the alms round helps laypeople practice?
check.why: Giving food each morning is a daily practice of generosity.

lessons.title: What a Visitor Sees
lessons.mainIdea: A temple visitor may see a shrine, offerings, and people bowing or chanting.
reading: When you walk into a Buddhist temple, you often see a *shrine* first. A statue of the Buddha sits in the center. It is placed high, as a sign of respect.
Around it are offerings: flowers, candles, incense and food. You may hear people chanting together. You may see people *bowing* before the statue. Many people sit on the floor.
Buddhists explain bowing in different ways. Many say they bow to show respect for the Buddha and his teaching. They say they are not bowing to the metal or stone itself.

words.d: a place set up to honor a holy person, often with a statue and offerings
bending the body or head to show respect

look.title: Inside the Hall
look.text: The hall is quiet. The Buddha statue sits on a high platform with eyes half closed. Candles glow on each side. A man kneels, puts his hands together and bows three times. Then he sits quietly.
look.prompt: What might the man say his bow means?

check.q: Why is the Buddha statue usually placed high?
choices: So it will not get dusty
Because it is too heavy for the floor
check.why: Placing the statue high shows respect.

check.q: What do many Buddhists say they are bowing to?
check.why: Many Buddhists say the bow honors the Buddha and the Dharma, not the material.

check.q: Which might you hear in a temple hall?
check.why: Chanting together is common in Buddhist temples.

lessons.title: Being a Respectful Guest
lessons.mainIdea: Visitors show respect by taking off shoes, speaking softly and following the hosts.
reading: Many temples ask guests to take off their shoes at the door. Floors in prayer halls are kept very clean. You might see rows of shoes by the entrance. Just follow what others do.
Guests speak softly. They do not point their feet at the Buddha statue or at monks. In many Asian cultures, pointing the feet is rude. A guest can sit with feet tucked to the side.
A *guest* does not have to bow or chant. Watching quietly is fine. The best thing a visitor can do is ask the hosts what is welcome. That is *respect*.

words.d: a visitor who is welcomed into someone else's place
showing care for people and what matters to them

look.title: Guest Checklist
rows: Keep feet pointed away from the shrine
Ask the hosts what is welcome
look.cite: Common guidance given by many Buddhist temples to visitors
look.prompt: Which step do you think is most important? Why?

check.q: What do many temples ask guests to do at the door?
check.why: Shoes come off to keep the hall clean.

check.q: Why should guests not point their feet at the Buddha statue?
choices: In many Asian cultures, it is rude
check.why: Pointing the feet is seen as disrespectful in many Asian cultures.

check.q: Must a guest bow or chant?
check.why: Guests may simply watch quietly and ask the hosts what is welcome.

lessons.title: One Buddhism, Many Faces
lessons.mainIdea: Chicago's temples show the many ways Buddhists practice, and none is ranked above another.
reading: In one city, you can find Shin, Zen, Thai, Vietnamese and Tibetan temples. Each has its own language, clothing and customs. Some are big, and some are small. Each one is a real place where families meet.
Yet they share some things. All honor the Buddha. All treasure the Dharma, his teaching. All have a sangha, a *community*. Buddhists call these the *Three Jewels*.
Scholars who study religion describe each group on its own terms. They do not say one is the true Buddhism. Learning about many temples helps us see the whole picture.

words.d: the Buddha, the Dharma and the Sangha, which all Buddhists honor
a group of people who share a practice or a life together

look.title: Two Children Compare
look.text: Ana goes to a Vietnamese temple. Kenji goes to a Shin temple. Ana says, 'We have monks in brown robes.' Kenji says, 'We have a minister and Sunday school.' Both say, 'We honor the Buddha.'
look.prompt: What is the same for Ana and Kenji? What is different?

check.q: What are the Three Jewels?
choices: The Buddha, the Dharma and the Sangha
check.why: Buddhists honor the Buddha, his teaching and the community as the Three Jewels.

check.q: How do scholars describe different Buddhist groups?
choices: By picking the one true group
Each on its own terms, without ranking
By counting only the biggest temple
check.why: Scholars describe traditions without saying one is the true Buddhism.

check.q: Which do all these temples share?
check.why: Languages and customs differ, but all honor the Buddha.

review.q: Who started the Buddhist Temple of Chicago in 1944?
choices: Rev. Gyomay Kubose and Japanese American families
review.why: Rev. Kubose and Japanese Americans leaving the camps founded it.

choices: The Buddhist Temple of Chicago opened
review.why: Buddhist speakers came to the 1893 Parliament in Chicago.

choices: Monks walking each morning to receive food
review.why: On the alms round, monks walk and laypeople give food.

review.q: What do many temples ask guests to take off?
review.why: Shoes come off at the door of many prayer halls.

review.q: Which word means the community of monks and nuns?
Why did many Vietnamese, Cambodian and Laotian families come to Illinois?
choices: They came as refugees after wars
They came to study in Tibet
review.why: Many came as refugees after the wars of the 1970s.

review.q: What do many Buddhists say bowing shows?
choices: Respect for the Buddha and his teaching
review.why: Buddhists often describe bowing as respect for the Buddha and the Dharma.

review.q: Which is the best guest behavior in a temple?
choices: Point your feet at the shrine
Ask the hosts what is welcome
review.why: Asking the hosts is a respectful way to be a guest.
